name: spectralnorm
axis: realistic whole program: f64 array indexing in a tight O(n^2) inner loop, plus a small leaf function (A(i,j)) called once per element
notes: Adapted from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game `spectralnorm` (matrix-free A/At multiplies, 10 power iterations, n=5500 — the reference N). Single-threaded everywhere: no rayon, no worker threads. ADAPTATION: prints through the same integer-scaling fmt9 as the other benchmarks instead of printf %.9f. JS uses Float64Array (what the reference JS entry uses, and the peer of VL's f64[] / Rust's Vec<f64>); Python uses a plain list of floats, no numpy. All four print 1.274224153 at n=5500 and agree at n=100 with the published reference (1.274219991). Scale-verified (O(n^2), n=2750 -> 5500 should be 4x): rust 0.277->1.286s, deno 0.537->2.063s, VL 0.717->2.666s, python 275->550 0.256->1.084s. Python's N is 550 (1/100 of the work). This is VL's WORST benchmark relative to JS (1.3-1.4x slower) — see the array-indexing finding: every f64[] element read reloads `backing` and `len` from the list header and does an explicit i32.ge_u + select bounds check in front of an array.get that already traps, and neither wasm-opt -O3 nor cranelift hoists them out of the loop. Final timings (min over all observations): rust 1.048s, deno 1.827s, VL 2.666s (prebuilt; 2.54x Rust, 1.46x deno), python(550) 1.011s. `vl build -O3` 2.470s (binaryen inlines aij, but the redundant per-access bounds check and the backing/len reloads survive).
